proxy_language: Unattested/unidentified culture: the name 'Iarnbòtrach' is Gaelic-looking (iarn 'iron' + a Gaelic-style suffix) and does not correspond to any attested culture or language in Russia/Central Asia/India. Best-supported proxy for a later (Period 6) steppe-to-Indian court culture in this region is Chagatai Turkic (Eastern Middle Turkic, Timurid/Mughal court language of Central Asia and India), written in Latin scholarly transliteration. A Persian-lexicon layer is typical of such courts.
proxy_rationale: No language called Iarnbòtrach is attested. The region label (Russia, Central Asia, India) and the court-period index point to Turco-Persian courts such as the Timurids and early Mughals. Chagatai is the best-documented court vernacular spanning that zone (Babur's Baburnama, Navai's works), with Persian as the high-prestige co-language. The link between the game culture and Chagatai is by region and period only; the culture name itself is unrelated to Turkic.
phonology: Chagatai (Eastern Middle Turkic), in scholarly transliteration. Consonants: p b t d k g q ġ (voiced uvular fricative/stop) c (affricate, often written č) j (ǰ) s z š f v/w h x (velar fricative, mostly in loans) m n ŋ (ñ) l r y. Vowels: a e i ı o ö u ü (with ē ō in some conventions). Vowel harmony: back/front (palatal) harmony governs suffixes, and rounding harmony operates partially; Perso-Arabic loans often break harmony. Stress is generally word-final.
phonotactics: Native syllable shapes: V, CV, VC, CVC, CVCC (CC only word-finally, e.g. -rt, -nč). No native initial consonant clusters (loans from Persian are epenthesized or accepted: e.g. Persian 'ustād' with prothetic vowels). Native words do not begin with r, l, n, ŋ, z (these occur only in loans). Voiced stops b d g are common initially in native words, and word-final voicing alternations occur in suffixation (-lAr, -dA/-tA). Words are mostly 2-3 syllables, with longer words formed by agglutination.
orthography: Scholarly Latin transliteration of Chagatai in the Turkological convention: ç or č for affricate, š for sh, j or ǰ for voiced affricate, ı for the back unrounded vowel, ö ü for front rounded vowels, ñ or ŋ for the velar nasal, ġ for voiced velar/uvular, q for uvular stop. For the game, a simplified Latin script is safest: a b c d e f g h i ı j k l m n o ö p q r s ş t u ü v y z, with vowel harmony respected in suffix choice.
morphology: Agglutinating, suffixing language. Roots are mostly monosyllabic, verbal or nominal, and noun stems are followed by plural -lAr (-lar/-ler), possessive suffixes (-ım/-im, -ı/-i/-sı/-si), case suffixes (genitive -nıŋ/-niŋ, accusative -nı/-ni, dative -ġa/-ge/-qa/-ke, locative -da/-de/-ta/-te, ablative -dın/-din/-tın/-tin) and derivational suffixes: -çı/-či (agent, 'maker/keeper of'), -lıq/-lik (abstract/collective/place), -lıġ/-lig (having, with), -sız/-siz (without), -ġan/-gen, -ış (nominalization), -ım. Verb derivation: -la- (denominal verb), -ġa- etc. No noun classes or grammatical gender.
compounding: Compounds are head-final: modifier + head. Two main patterns: (1) bare nominal compound: modifier + head with the head optionally taking the 3rd-person possessive -(s)ı (Turkish-style izafet / 'tamlama'): e.g. 'tağ yol' mountain road; 'altun yurt' golden home; (2) genitive + possessed: X-nıŋ Y-ı 'Y of X'. Persian ezafe constructions (head + -i + modifier, e.g. 'bāġ-i bihišt' garden of paradise) are used in learned/court register for loanword phrases. Agent names: noun + -çı (e.g. 'temürçi' ironworker, 'ātçı' horse-keeper). Place names often use -lıq/-zar/-stan/-ābād as loan suffixes.
noun_phrase_order: Modifier-head order throughout: adjective before noun, genitive before possessed noun, demonstrative/numeral before noun, relative clauses (participial) before noun. In Persian-register phrases the ezafe construction reverses this to head-modifier (e.g. 'šāh-i muʿaẓẓam' 'the great king'). Plural marking only once on the noun; adjectives are uninflected.
